title: The slow path and the LOH
sub: When a pointer bump is not enough and who starts a collection
cards/0/title: When the fast path will not do
cards/0/body:
Pointer bumping works for most objects. But in some cases the JIT or the fast path itself sends the allocation to the collector — down the slow path:

  • the chunk ran out — the object did not fit in what was left;
  • the object is large — 85,000 bytes or more, it belongs in the LOH, not generation 0;
  • the type has a finalizer — the object must also be registered in the finalization queue.

The first case is decided at allocation time. A finalizer and the size of an ordinary object are visible to the JIT in advance: for such types it calls the slow helper right away. The size of an array is known only at run time, so a large array is sent down the slow path by the helper itself.
cards/0/deep: You can see this in CEEInfo::getNewHelperStatic (jitinterface.cpp): the slow helper CORINFO_HELP_NEWFAST is the default, and the fast CORINFO_HELP_NEWSFAST is chosen only if the type has no finalizer, is not a COM object and is smaller than LARGE_OBJECT_SIZE. For arrays the size is known only at run time, so the helper itself checks the threshold.
cards/1/q: Which allocations always take the slow path? Select all.
cards/1/explain: A finalizer is a reason for the slow path, and a double[20,000] weighs over 160,000 bytes and goes to the LOH. A record is an ordinary class without a finalizer. A 10-character string is a small object, fast path.
cards/2/body:
The slow path is a collector function whose job is to give the thread a new chunk. Roughly in this order it:

  • takes the heap lock — chunks are handed out to all threads from a shared place;
  • checks the generation 0 budget: how much more can be allocated before the next collection;
  • looks for room: a free block left over from the last collection (the free list), or an untouched part of a generation 0 region, and if there is none — takes a new region;
  • zeroes the chunk, turns the tail of the old chunk into a free object and updates the thread's alloc_ptr/alloc_limit.

That is hundreds or thousands of instructions, but it happens once per many allocations.
cards/2/deep: In Server GC each core has its own heap, and the slow path can move a thread to another, less loaded heap (balancing). Small and large objects use different locks: more_space_lock_soh and more_space_lock_uoh in gc.cpp. So a thread allocating large arrays does not get in the way of threads with small objects — but threads with large arrays do get in each other's way.
cards/3/q: Put the slow-path steps in order
cards/3/items/0: The object did not fit in the rest of the chunk
cards/3/items/3: Find a free piece and zero it
cards/3/items/4: Give the thread a new alloc_ptr and alloc_limit
cards/3/explain: The slow path starts with a fast-path miss and ends with the thread getting a fresh chunk, where the object is allocated with an ordinary bump. If the budget is exhausted, a collection happens between the third and fourth steps.
cards/4/title: The budget: new starts the collection
cards/4/body:
The collector does not watch the clock. Generation 0 has an allocation budget — how many bytes may be allocated before the next collection. Every chunk handed out is charged against it.

When the budget is exhausted, the slow path starts a collection right on this thread, and a new that normally costs nanoseconds waits for the collection to finish. All other managed threads are stopped meanwhile.

The key consequence: collection frequency is proportional to the allocation rate. Half the garbage per second means half as many generation 0 collections.
cards/4/deep: The budget is not fixed: the collector recomputes it after every collection — based on how many objects survived — within a lower and an upper bound. The initial size of generation 0 depends on the CPU cache size (L3), and is larger for Server GC. Besides allocation, collections are triggered by an explicit GC.Collect, a low-memory signal from the OS and some internal events — more on triggers in the unit "How a collection works".
cards/5/q: A service allocates 2 GB of short-lived objects per second, and almost all die in generation 0. What will you see in the counters?
cards/5/options/0: Many generation 0 collections per second with a small heap
cards/5/options/1: A heap growing by 2 GB per second until OutOfMemoryException
cards/5/options/3: Nothing: the collector does not account for short-lived objects
cards/5/explain: Every few megabytes of budget there is a generation 0 collection. Dead objects cost nothing to mark, so collections are short and the heap does not grow. The price is frequent thread suspensions: cut them down and the gain shows immediately.
cards/5/wrong/1: Garbage does not pile up: each generation 0 collection reclaims its memory.
cards/5/wrong/2: Full collections are triggered by older generations and the LOH filling up, and almost nothing reaches them here.
cards/6/body:
An object of 85,000 bytes or more — the whole object counts, header included — is allocated not in generation 0 but in the LOH (large object heap). In practice it is almost always an array, or a long string: a string of 50,000 characters weighs over 100,000 bytes.

How such an allocation works:

  • always the slow path, through its own lock;
  • room is found among the LOH free blocks, and the whole object is zeroed — for a megabyte array that is noticeable work;
  • the LOH has its own budget. Once it is exhausted, a generation 2 collection runs — that is, a full one.

The structure of the LOH itself is covered in the unit "Inside the heap".
cards/6/deep: The threshold can be changed with the System.GC.LOHThreshold setting in runtimeconfig.json (since .NET Core 3.0) — only upward from 85,000. By default the LOH is not compacted; free blocks are reused via a list, so alternating arrays of different sizes cause fragmentation; a one-off compaction is enabled with GCSettings.LargeObjectHeapCompactionMode. Then and now: in 32-bit .NET Framework, double arrays of 1000 elements or more went to the LOH below the threshold — for 8-byte alignment.
cards/7/q: Which of these objects lands in the LOH (64-bit process)?
cards/7/explain: A char takes 2 bytes, so a 50,000-character string is over 100,000 bytes. int[20,000] is about 80,000 bytes, object[10,000] is 10,000 references of 8 bytes, also about 80,000. List<long>(5,000) is a small object plus an internal array of 40,000 bytes. All three are below the threshold.
cards/7/wrong/2: A reference in a 64-bit process is 8 bytes: 80,000 bytes plus the header, the 85,000 threshold is not reached.
cards/7/wrong/3: The List itself is a small object, and its long[5,000] array is about 40,000 bytes.
cards/8/title: A temporary large buffer is an expensive habit
cards/8/body:
A common sight in services: every request allocates a one-megabyte buffer, which is garbage a millisecond later. From the code's point of view, no big deal. From the collector's point of view:

  • every buffer is a slow path plus zeroing a megabyte;
  • the buffers quickly eat the LOH budget;
  • each time it runs out — a full collection that walks the whole heap, not just young objects.

In the counters this shows up as frequent generation 2 collections while hardly any old objects are added. The cure is reusing the buffer — a pool (lesson 4).
cards/9/q: A service runs several full collections per second. Which line is the prime suspect?
cards/9/explain: A megabyte per request is the LOH: slow path, zeroing and fast exhaustion of the LOH budget, after which a generation 2 collection runs. The dictionary and the string are small short-lived objects that die in generation 0.
cards/10/q: Match the event and its consequence
cards/10/pairs/0/1: The slow path hands out a new one
cards/10/pairs/1/1: A generation 0 collection right inside new
cards/10/pairs/3/1: Registered in the finalization queue on creation
cards/10/pairs/4/1: Straight to the LOH, bypassing generation 0
